schemaDesign.rationale:
DESIGN CHOICES, GROUPED:

1. SUPERSET vs least-common-denominator: Used SUPERSET. Reasoning: only DOB
   (HCSO+MDCR only), full address (OCFL only), mugshot URL pattern (varies
   per sheriff), and the alternate-ID columns (obtsNumber/jacketNumber/idsNumber)
   are sheriff-specific. Making those nullable is cheap; future sheriffs can
   slot in without an ALTER TABLE. Charges JSON shape was unified across all 6
   to a single schema (statute/description/severity/bondAmount/bondType/...)
   even though no single sheriff exposes all 7 — null-tolerant fields are
   trivially cheaper than a polymorphic JSON.

2. UNIQUE constraint = (sheriffSlug, bookingId): every probe confirmed a
   per-booking unique ID at source (JSO incarcerationId, HCSO bookingNumber,
   OCFL bookingNumber, BSO JMS_NUMBER, MDCR JailNumber, PBSO Booking Number).
   Coercing all to string + scoping by sheriffSlug guarantees collision-free
   even if two counties ever pick the same numeric. This mirrors the
   ParcelSale.unique([countyFips, apn, saleDate, source]) pattern (re-scrapes
   idempotent via UPSERT on the unique key).

3. countyFips kept separate from sheriffSlug (1:1 currently) because:
   - matcher joins against Parcel.countyFips, not a sheriff slug
   - future multi-sheriff counties (e.g. county sheriff + municipal jail)
     are possible
   - the cost of one extra String column is zero

4. Charges as Json[] not separate table: see additionalModelsNeeded for
   the full rationale. tl;dr: ~440K charge rows/yr is sub-threshold for the
   join overhead, and our query patterns (filter by topChargeSeverity, sum
   totalBond, count chargeCount) are all denormalized onto InmateBooking
   for index-only scans.

5. Matcher state fields LIVE on InmateBooking (vs a separate JailMatch
   table): keeps the hot-path read (`SELECT * FROM InmateBooking WHERE
   parcelId = ?`) a single index hit. The cost is that re-running the
   matcher rewrites the InmateBooking row, but matcher passes are infrequent
   (daily) and the updatedAt timestamp gives us an honest "last touched" audit.

6. legalRisk default "yellow" not "green": every one of the 6 sheriffs has
   at least one yellow trigger (captcha gate, name-required search form,
   antiforgery token, citrix-fronted IIS, or HTML-fragile parsing).
   Per CLAUDE memory §5.1 of FL-COVERAGE-PLAN.md, yellow sources need the
   hardening checklist applied — this column makes a one-SQL purge possible
   if a cease-and-desist arrives.

7. isExempt as boolean + exemptReason + exemptAt (not a separate
   ExemptRedaction table): exemption events are sparse and per-row. A
   separate table would 99.9% join to empty. Boolean + reason string is
   cheaper and lets the API layer filter with one WHERE clause.

8. release tracking: releaseDate nullable on the same row. JSO publishes
   a separate ReleaseLog endpoint, but the matching is by incarcerationId
   which becomes our bookingId — UPDATE WHERE bookingId=? is cleaner than
   a sibling JailReleaseEvent table. The lastSeenAt column captures "we
   re-scraped and they're still in" without needing a release-event row.

9. mugshot storage: pointer-only on this row, binary in R2. OCFL's
   inline-base64 approach would 5x our PG storage cost for this table at
   175 rows/day × 65KB.

10. NO foreign key on parcelId: the matcher is allowed to fail-open. If a
    parcel row is deleted (rare — only on county re-import) we don't want
    the InmateBooking deleted with it. matchConfidence + matchMethod give
    us enough diagnostic info to rerun the matcher.

11. Normalization moved out of DB into application code (the spec): keeps
    the schema portable and lets us evolve the normalizer (e.g. add Hispanic
    surname handling for MDCR) without an ALTER. The normalizedName column
    is just the stored output of the latest normalizer version — re-run on
    a schema-pass when the normalizer changes.

WHAT WE DELIBERATELY DID NOT INCLUDE:
  - Geocoded lat/long on the address fields (OCFL is the only address source;
    geocoding belongs in a downstream enrichment, not the raw capture).
  - A "freshness window" expiration column. HCSO's 90-day rolling window is
    handled by the scraper's not-seen-since logic and a rollup query, not a
    persisted TTL.
  - A separate ChargeSeverity enum. FL statute classifications vary too
    much (Mxx / Fxx / civil infraction / county ordinance) to lock into an
    enum that early; keep as String, taxonomy in app code, promote later.

CROSS-CHECK WITH PROBE DATA:
  - JSO: incarcerationId → bookingId ✓, no DOB/address ✓, charges array ✓,
    overallBailAmount → totalBond (× 100 for cents) ✓
  - HCSO: bookingNumber → bookingId ✓, DOB present ✓, no address ✓,
    SearchIncludeDetails toggle drives charges/bond ✓
  - OCFL: bookingNumber → bookingId ✓, age not DOB (age column on row) ✓,
    full address ✓, base64 PNG → R2 ✓
  - BSO: JMS_NUMBER → bookingId ✓, no DOB ✓, no bond in list (detail
    enrichment fills) ✓
  - MDCR: JailNumber → bookingId ✓, DOB present ✓, IDS → idsNumber ✓,
    no address ✓, warrant-case detail block → charges array ✓
  - PBSO: Booking Number → bookingId ✓, no DOB ✓, OBTS → obtsNumber ✓,
    Jacket Number → jacketNumber ✓, charges block with bond per charge ✓,
    Release Date column → releaseDate ✓
openQuestions: Should we promote topChargeSeverity to a Prisma enum once the FL classification list (M1/M2/F1/F2/F3/CT/CI) is locked? Recommendation: keep as String until we have 30 days of data and can see the actual cardinality.

JSO Person.arrest[] doesn't explicitly include arrest/booking timestamp in the SPA constructor — production scraper must confirm the field name on first live solve. Schema is unaffected (bookingDate is required and the scraper must source it from somewhere).

BSO InmateDetail/{JMS_NUMBER} schema is unprobed — its DOB/charges/bond shape needs a Phase-2 captcha-solved seed search before the BSO scraper writes rows. Schema doesn't need to change; just confirms the existing nullable fields are populated correctly.

Cross-sheriff dedupe: the same person re-arrested across counties (Miami-Dade then Broward) will create two InmateBooking rows — by design — but the matcher should link them via (normalizedName, dateOfBirth) where available, or (normalizedName, obtsNumber) where PBSO exposes it. Confirm we want this collapsed at the matcher layer, not the schema layer.

Mugshot retention policy: do we keep R2 mugshots indefinitely or expire after N days for §119.071 hygiene? Schema supports both (mugshotCapturedAt timestamp + a cron-driven purge), but the policy decision is upstream.

matcherDesign.normalizationRules:
{
  "principle": "Both sides normalize to a canonical {firstName, middleInitial, lastName, suffix} + nameKey hash. NEVER mutate source rows — store normalized columns alongside (denormalized for join speed). Run the same normalizer on both pipelines so behavior cannot drift.",
  "sharedSteps": [
    "1. Uppercase everything, NFKD-unicode-normalize, strip diacritics (CHÁVEZ -> CHAVEZ — critical for Miami-Dade where ~68% of names are Hispanic).",
    "2. Strip all punctuation except apostrophe-in-name (O'BRIEN keeps the '), commas, hyphens, periods. Replace with single space.",
    "3. Collapse multiple spaces to single space and trim.",
    "4. Tokenize on whitespace into ordered tokens.",
    "5. Remove suffix tokens from the name stream BUT preserve them on the canonical record: {JR, SR, II, III, IV, V, 2ND, 3RD, 4TH, ESQ, MD, PHD, DDS, DO}. Suffix is a tiebreaker, not part of the match key.",
    "6. Remove single-letter middle-name tokens AFTER recording them as middleInitial. 'JOHN A SMITH' -> first=JOHN, mi=A, last=SMITH.",
    "7. Build nameKey = `${lastName}|${firstName}` (NO middle, NO suffix). This is the coarse hash for the in-memory join.",
    "8. Build fullKey = `${lastName}|${firstName}|${middleInitial||''}` for the precise-match tier."
  ],
  "inmateSide": {
    "supportedFormats": [
      "JSO: server returns firstName, middleName, lastName, suffix as separate fields — use directly, no parsing.",
      "OCFL: `NAME` field is 'LAST, FIRST MIDDLE [SUFFIX] ' with trailing whitespace. Split on first ', '. Right-side trim. Tokenize the right side; if last token is in SUFFIX_SET, peel it.",
      "MDCR: `BookingName` td text is 'LAST, FIRST [MIDDLE]' — same split-on-comma path.",
      "PBSO: 'STEVENS, JUSTIN EDWARD' — same.",
      "BSO: LAST_NAME / FIRST_NAME / MIDDLE_NAME are separate fields.",
      "HCSO: search-form returns 'Last Name, First Name' string in result table — same split-on-comma."
    ],
    "edgeCases": [
      "OCFL ZIPCODE-style trailing whitespace shows up in NAME too — always trim each token.",
      "MDCR multi-word first names ('MARY ANN SMITH' on a LAST,FIRST schema is ambiguous) — keep the rule: first token of right-side = firstName, last token of right-side = middleName ONLY if it is single-letter or two tokens exist; otherwise concatenate middle tokens with space.",
      "Hyphenated last names ('SMITH-JONES, JOHN') — keep the hyphen-joined token as a single lastName. Also produce a SECONDARY match candidate splitting on hyphen ('SMITH', 'JONES' each tried as lastName) for fuzzy tier.",
      "Name-with-apostrophe: store both 'OBRIEN' and 'O'BRIEN' as alias candidates — Florida tax rolls inconsistently strip the apostrophe.",
      "Single-name inmates (no middle): middleInitial = null, do not synthesize.",
      "All-caps middle names longer than 1 char (e.g. 'JOHN ALEXANDER SMITH'): middleInitial = 'A' (first char of middle), also store fullMiddle = 'ALEXANDER' for confidence boost on exact-middle match."
    ]
  },
  "parcelSide": {
    "preprocessSteps": [
      "1. Detect-and-flag corporate/entity ownership BEFORE attempting personal-name parse. Set parcel.ownerCorporate = true and SKIP downstream matching entirely if ownerName matches any of: /\\b(LLC|L\\.L\\.C\\.|LP|L\\.P\\.|LLP|INC|INCORPORATED|CORP|CORPORATION|CO|COMPANY|TRUST|TRUSTEE|TR|REVOCABLE|IRREVOCABLE|LIVING\\s+TRUST|FAMILY\\s+TRUST|ESTATE\\s+OF|EST\\s+OF|FOUNDATION|CHURCH|MINISTRIES|CITY\\s+OF|COUNTY\\s+OF|STATE\\s+OF|HOA|ASSOCIATION|ASSN|PARTNERS|HOLDINGS|GROUP|PROPERTIES|REALTY|INVESTMENTS|CAPITAL|VENTURES|HOLDINGS)\\b/. This is the single biggest false-positive guard — 'SMITH HOLDINGS LLC' on a parcel must never bind to inmate 'JOHN SMITH'.",
      "2. Strip ownership-modifier tokens from the name stream (do NOT skip the record, just clean the string): 'ET AL', 'ET UX', 'ET VIR', 'H/W' (husband/wife), 'W/H', 'JT WROS', 'JTWROS', 'TIC' (tenants-in-common), 'TBE' (tenants-by-entirety), 'LE' / 'LIFE ESTATE' / 'L/E', 'REMAINDERMAN', 'C/O' (care-of — keep the c/o name separate as alternate match), 'FBO' (for-benefit-of), 'POA', 'CUSTODIAN', 'TTEE', 'TTEES'.",
      "3. Split on '&' or ' AND ' to produce TWO+ candidate owners per parcel. 'SMITH JOHN & SMITH MARY' -> [SMITH JOHN, SMITH MARY]. Each becomes its own join key — both should be searchable.",
      "4. Detect FL DOR last-name-first vs first-name-first ordering. FL DOR NAL bulk format is overwhelmingly `LAST FIRST [MIDDLE]` (no comma). Heuristic: if no comma present AND first token is in COMMON_LAST_NAMES_FL (top-5000 surname dictionary), assume LAST FIRST ordering. Else assume FIRST LAST. This heuristic is wrong ~3-5% of the time — produce BOTH orderings as match candidates at lower confidence.",
      "5. After parse, run the same sharedSteps normalization."
    ],
    "examples": [
      "'SMITH JOHN A' -> last=SMITH, first=JOHN, mi=A, suffix=null, ownerCorporate=false",
      "'SMITH JOHN III' -> last=SMITH, first=JOHN, mi=null, suffix=III, ownerCorporate=false",
      "'SMITH JOHN ET AL' -> last=SMITH, first=JOHN, etAl=true (flag — second owner unknown, lower confidence)",
      "'SMITH JOHN LIFE ESTATE' -> last=SMITH, first=JOHN, lifeEstate=true (flag — name is likely the deceased, lower confidence)",
      "'SMITH JOHN & SMITH MARY' -> [{last=SMITH,first=JOHN}, {last=SMITH,first=MARY}] — two candidates emitted",
      "'SMITH FAMILY TRUST' -> ownerCorporate=true, SKIP",
      "'JOHN SMITH HOLDINGS LLC' -> ownerCorporate=true, SKIP",
      "'CITY OF JACKSONVILLE' -> ownerCorporate=true, SKIP"
    ]
  },
  "denormalizedColumns": "Add to Parcel: ownerCorporate Boolean, ownerNormalized Json[] (array of {last, first, mi, suffix, nameKey, fullKey}). Add to JailBooking: nameNormalized Json {last, first, mi, suffix, nameKey, fullKey}, dobBucket String? (YYYY-MM if DOB present, e.g. '1977-08'), ageAtBooking Int? (when only age available, e.g. OCFL). Indexed (countyFips, nameKey) on Parcel for fast hash join.",
  "languageNotes": "Hispanic compound surnames (RODRIGUEZ-MARTINEZ, RODRIGUEZ MARTINEZ, RODRIGUEZ DE LA CRUZ) common in Miami-Dade. Emit ALL candidate split-points as alternate nameKeys: ['RODRIGUEZ MARTINEZ', 'RODRIGUEZ', 'MARTINEZ']. Particle words ('DE', 'LA', 'DEL', 'VAN', 'VON', 'MC', 'MAC', 'O', 'DA', 'DOS') keep with adjacent token. 'DE LA CRUZ' stays as a single lastName token in the primary key, plus 'CRUZ' as a secondary nameKey."
}

strategyLadder.description: Exact match on (nameKey, countyFips) AND (DOB-derived age range) AND ownerCorporate=false. Highest precision; only available when sheriff publishes DOB (MDCR, HCSO) or we can derive age (OCFL exposes age in years). Match window: DOB must match within +/- 0 years if YYYY-MM-DD known; +/- 1 year if only year known. Also requires fullKey match (last+first+mi) when mi is available on both sides.
strategyLadder.requirements: DOB or age present on inmate row; parcel has ownerCorporate=false; in-county parcel exists at nameKey.

strategyLadder.description: Exact match on (fullKey, countyFips) [last+first+middleInitial] AND ownerCorporate=false. Used when DOB is NOT available (JSO, BSO, PBSO). Requires the inmate to have a middleInitial AND the parcel to have a middleInitial AND they match. Cuts ambiguity by ~10x vs nameKey alone — 'JOHN SMITH' is common, 'JOHN A SMITH' is rare.
strategyLadder.requirements: Both sides have middleInitial; ownerCorporate=false; exactly ONE parcel matches in-county.

strategyLadder.description: Exact (nameKey, countyFips) match AND ownerCorporate=false AND the inmate's nameKey appears on EXACTLY ONE non-corporate parcel in the county. Uniqueness is the precision lever — common names like 'JOHN SMITH' get rejected here because >1 parcel matches.
strategyLadder.requirements: Exactly 1 candidate parcel after corporate filter and county filter; no DOB needed; no middleInitial needed.

strategyLadder.description: Exact (nameKey, countyFips) AND parcel.situsCity matches the booking-record city (when sheriff publishes city — OCFL does via STREET field; PBSO via arrestingAgency). Tightens the join when inmate name matches multiple parcels but only one is in a plausible city.
strategyLadder.requirements: Sheriff record exposes a city signal (booking address OR arresting-agency-jurisdiction); >1 parcel at nameKey but exactly 1 in matching city.

strategyLadder.description: Exact (nameKey, countyFips), >1 candidate parcel, no city signal. Bind to the parcel where parcel.situsAddress == parcel.ownerMailingAddress (primary residence / homestead-style heuristic) IF exactly one candidate satisfies it. Otherwise emit AMBIGUOUS.
strategyLadder.requirements: Multiple candidates; exactly one has homestead-style ownership signal.

strategyLadder.description: Levenshtein <=2 on lastName AND exact firstName AND ownerCorporate=false AND unique-in-county. Catches OCR-style typos and apostrophe stripping ('OBRIEN' vs 'OBRIAN', 'SMITH' vs 'SMYTH'). Bounded by edit-distance to avoid 'SMITH' -> 'JONES'.
strategyLadder.requirements: Unique candidate after fuzzy; not used when an S1-S5 candidate already exists.

strategyLadder.description: For hyphenated/compound surnames, try each half as standalone lastName. 'SMITH-JONES, JOHN' tries lastName='SMITH' and lastName='JONES'. Requires exact firstName + uniqueness + non-corporate.
strategyLadder.requirements: Inmate or parcel has hyphen/space-compound lastName; alternate-half produces a unique non-corporate hit.

strategyLadder.description: Anything that survives to this rung is rejected — no parcelId bound, matchConfidence=null, matchStatus='AMBIGUOUS' or 'NO_MATCH'. Surface as distress-signal-without-property-binding (still useful for name+county count aggregates).

matcherDesign.ambiguityPolicy:
{
  "rule": "When two or more parcels survive at the SAME strategy tier, NEVER bind. Set matchStatus='AMBIGUOUS', store candidateParcelIds Json[] (max 5), matchConfidence=null.",
  "neverPickLowest": "Explicitly do NOT 'pick the lowest-confidence one' or 'pick the first one' — that's a precision-killer. Surface in admin review tray.",
  "exceptionFamilyOwnership": "If 2 parcels match and BOTH have the same ownerMailingAddress (same person owns 2 properties, one rental + one primary), bind to the one where situsAddress == ownerMailingAddress (primary residence). Confidence drops to 0.65 (PROVISIONAL).",
  "reviewTray": "Build a /app/admin/match-review page that lists AMBIGUOUS rows with candidate parcels side-by-side, lets an analyst manually bind (writes matchStatus='MANUAL', matchConfidence=1.0, matchedByUserId). Manual bindings are sticky and survive future re-matches.",
  "sensitiveOccupationFilter": "Defense-in-depth §119.071 filter: if the bound parcel owner's mailing address matches a known LEO/judge/prosecutor block-list (separate table — to be populated by ops), force matchStatus='SUPPRESSED' and never surface."
}
matcherDesign.performanceApproach:
{
  "scale": "Per-county Parcel rows: Miami-Dade ~970k, Broward ~750k, Palm Beach ~620k, Hillsborough ~580k, Duval ~430k, Orange ~510k. Daily inmate volume per county: 60-180. So per-county join is ~100 inmates x ~700k parcels (worst case). Naive nested-loop = 70M comparisons/day across all 6 counties — unacceptable. Indexed hash join = ~600 hash lookups/day — trivial.",
  "indexStrategy": "Add Prisma index @@index([countyFips, ownerCorporate, nameKey]) on Parcel. Composite PG B-tree handles all of: corporate-filter, county-filter, name-lookup in a single scan. ALSO add GIN trigram index `CREATE INDEX parcel_name_trgm ON \"flipops\".\"Parcel\" USING gin (\"ownerName\" gin_trgm_ops);` for S6 fuzzy tier (raw SQL via prisma.$executeRaw — Prisma migrations can't express it cleanly).",
  "inMemoryHotPath": "For the daily batch matcher, load per-county owner-name index into memory ONCE at job start: Map<nameKey, ParcelLite[]>. ParcelLite = {parcelId, countyFips, fullKey, situsCity, ownerMailingAddress, situsAddress, suffix}. Memory budget ~970k * ~120 bytes = ~120MB for Miami-Dade — fits comfortably in a Node process. Rebuild map nightly at 02:00 ET (after the DOR ingest catch-up window).",
  "incrementalPath": "For the per-scrape-tick matcher (fires after each sheriff scrape), use Prisma indexed lookup directly: `prisma.parcel.findMany({where: {countyFips, ownerCorporate: false, ownerNormalized: {path: ['$[*].nameKey'], array_contains: [nameKey]}}, take: 6})` — `take: 6` because we don't care past 5 candidates (we'll reject as ambiguous anyway). Postgres jsonb-path GIN gives sub-10ms lookup at this scale.",
  "batchSize": "Inmate-side batches of 500 — small enough to keep one Postgres transaction open per batch without bloating WAL, large enough to amortize Prisma overhead.",
  "concurrency": "Single-threaded per county to avoid Postgres connection blow-up. Cross-county can parallelize (6 counties = 6 workers). Total daily compute budget: <2 minutes wall-clock for all FL top-6.",
  "neverFullTableScan": "Cardinal sin guard: every match query MUST include countyFips in the WHERE clause. Add a Prisma middleware that throws if a match query is missing it."
}
matcherDesign.matcherInvocationPolicy:
{
  "trigger": "Hybrid — runs in BOTH modes, designed so the system is correct regardless of which fires first:",
  "tier1_onScrape": "Fires synchronously at the END of each sheriff scrape job (after upsert into JailBooking, before the scrape job marks itself succeeded). Only re-matches the rows JUST upserted (newly seen incarcerationId OR existing row where booking/release date changed). This is the 'low-latency' path — keeps the lead UI fresh within minutes of an arrest. Latency budget: <5 sec per 100 bookings.",
  "tier2_nightlyReconcile": "Cron at 03:30 ET (after DOR catch-up at 02:00 and tax-delinquent refresh at 03:00). Re-runs the matcher against the ENTIRE last-30-day JailBooking window in case (a) a Parcel was newly ingested overnight, (b) a Parcel's ownerName changed via new sale (see re-match), (c) the matching code itself changed. Idempotent — same inputs always produce same outputs; uses matchStatus='MANUAL' as a sticky lock.",
  "tier3_onParcelSale": "Fires when ParcelSale.unique(countyFips, apn, saleDate, source) emits a NEW row. Re-matches any JailBooking from the last 365 days against the SOLD parcel (both old nameKey and new nameKey). Why 365: an arrest 6 months before a forced-sale is a strong distress signal we want to retrospectively bind. Implemented as a Prisma post-create hook on ParcelSale.",
  "neverMatchOn": "Bookings older than 365 days (signal stale, false-positive risk grows). Bookings with matchStatus='MANUAL' (never overwrite human judgment). Parcels where ownerCorporate=true (skip entirely).",
  "auditTrail": "Every match write goes to a JailBookingMatchLog table: {bookingId, parcelId, strategy, confidence, candidateCount, createdAt, batchId}. Lets us answer 'why was this booking bound to that parcel' six months later and lets us re-run with new logic by replaying logs.",
  "registrySourceKey": "Each sheriff scraper gets a ScrapeRegistry row with sourceKey='{slug}-jail-bookings' (e.g. 'jso-jail-bookings'). The post-scrape matcher reads this key to know which countyFips to scope to — single source of truth, no hardcoded county lists in the matcher."
}
openQuestions: Cross-county owners — a Tampa resident (Hillsborough) often owns a rental in Orlando (Orange). Should the matcher ever search OUTSIDE the booking county? Strawman: no for v1 (precision-first); add a Tier 2 cross-county pass in v2 once we have skip-trace confidence data to validate it doesn't false-match.

DOB granularity — JSO/BSO suppress DOB entirely, OCFL gives only age-in-years, MDCR/HCSO give full DOB, PBSO suppresses. How aggressively should we treat age-only as a tiebreaker? Strawman: age-only narrows from S2/S3 down to {parcel.ownerName + (currentYear - age) within +/- 1} when we can infer parcel.ownerAge from a separate source (FL voter rolls? Not in scope yet).

Spouse/co-owner bindings — when parcel ownerName is 'SMITH JOHN & SMITH MARY' and inmate is 'SMITH MARY', bind to the same parcel as we would for 'SMITH JOHN'? Strawman: yes; emit BOTH as separate JailBookingMatch rows pointing at the same parcelId with role='CO_OWNER'.

PBSO city-of-arrest signal — arrestingAgency '34-BOYNTON BEACH' implies city Boynton Beach. Build a code->city lookup table? Strawman: yes — encode as constant in lib/sheriffs/pbso/agencies.ts, used by S4.

MDCR enumeration coverage — surname-dictionary sweep misses ~10-30% of names. Do we accept that coverage gap, or push for FL DOR API/CCTV access? Strawman: accept for v1; add dynamic dictionary expansion from observed surnames per the probe note.

Re-match window on ParcelSale — 365 days is a guess. Should it be tunable per-strategy (S1-DOB match: 730 days OK; S5-heuristic: 90 days only)? Strawman: yes, make it a per-strategy config in MATCH_RULES constant.

Manual-bind UX — does the analyst see inmate mugshot + parcel address side-by-side? Strawman: yes, but mugshot view is gated behind a 'confirm I am acting in a permissible-purpose context' click (§119 / dignity posture).

Mugshot retention — we capture mugshots to R2 (per JSO probe), but if a record is later sealed/expunged, we have no auto-takedown signal. Should we expire mugshots at 90 days by default (matches HCSO's public-visibility policy)? Strawman: yes; cron job that deletes mugshots older than 90 days unless the booking has a matched parcelId with active outreach.

Score weighting — probe explicitly recommends a LOW weight (+5 not +20) on jail-booking distress signal due to fuzzy join. Confirm with product: is +5 to the distress score correct, or should it be a binary BADGE without contributing to the numeric score? Strawman: badge + 0 score in v1 (most conservative), revisit after 60 days of false-positive feedback data.

scoreWeights.justification: Still in jail with unpaid bond is THE highest-urgency liquidity signal in the consumer-asset universe — someone is literally locked up until they raise cash. Sits just below Pre-Foreclosure (25) and Auction (25) because (a) those have a hard legal deadline that forces a property sale, whereas a bond can be paid from many cash sources (family, bail bondsman 10%, credit), and (b) name-only matching to Parcel.ownerName has higher false-match risk than APN-keyed foreclosure data. Tied conceptually with Lien/Judgment (20) but ranked 2pts higher because the cash-need clock is hours/days, not 90+ days.

Released after posting cash bond means $1k–$50k+ just exited household reserves in the last 30 days. Equivalent in motivation to OUT_OF_STATE_OWNER (15) or INHERITED (15) — they're financially stressed but not under acute time pressure. The 10% bail-bondsman fee scenario is also captured here since it's still a non-recoverable cash hit.

Released on recognizance = no cash drained. Below the LOW tier (5pt floor for FREE_CLEAR, CORPORATE_OWNED). Only contributes a tiny ambient stress signal because pending criminal proceedings still imply legal-fee exposure, court dates, possible job loss. Keep below 5 so a single ROR booking alone cannot push a property into a higher grade band.

Two-or-more bookings in 12 months (tracked via inmateNumber/IDS persistent IDs from JSO, MDCR, OCFL) signals pattern of legal-system entanglement → recurring bail/legal-fee drain → chronic liquidity stress. Sized between QUIT_CLAIM (5) and HIGH_EQUITY (10). Only applies when there are >=2 confirmed bookings; does not stack on top of ACTIVE_BOND_IN_CUSTODY (compounding rule below).

Modifier on top of ACTIVE_BOND_IN_CUSTODY or POSTED_CASH_BOND_RECENT — caps the bond-channel contribution. When the bond is $25k+ (NO BOND felonies often aren't financially-relievable so these are excluded), the liquidity gap is materially larger. Treat as a +5 booster, not a standalone signal.

aggregationDesign.compoundingRules: "Bond signals are MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE within the jail channel — only the HIGHEST-weight jail signal applies per owner, never additive within channel. Specifically: if ACTIVE_BOND_IN_CUSTODY is true, ignore POSTED_CASH_BOND_RECENT and RELEASED_ROR for the same person. HIGH_BOND_AMOUNT_OVER_25K is the only stackable jail modifier (+5 booster on top of either ACTIVE or POSTED). RECIDIVISM is stackable IFF the active/recent booking is not already in scope (prevents double-counting the current event). CROSS-CHANNEL compounding with existing signals is ADDITIVE with a category cap: jail-channel total contribution is capped at 30 points (ACTIVE_BOND 22 + HIGH_BOND 5 + RECIDIVISM 8 would be 35 → capped to 30) to prevent jail signals from dominating the 0–100 scale. When jail + tax-delinquency + pre-foreclosure all hit the same parcel, that's a near-certain motivated seller — let it stack but the final score still caps at 100 per existing algorithm. Multiplicative compounding rejected: scoring is intentionally interpretable line-by-line for the score-breakdown tooltip; multiplicative math hides which signal drove the grade."
aggregationDesign.uiCopy: "Investor-facing badge text (in leads list and detail drawer): 'Acute liquidity signal' for ACTIVE_BOND_IN_CUSTODY (22pts), 'Recent liquidity event' for POSTED_CASH_BOND_RECENT (15pts), 'Elevated cash-motivation indicator' for RECIDIVISM_MULTIPLE_BOOKINGS_12MO (8pts), and the jail channel is hidden entirely from the investor when only RELEASED_ROR fires (4pts is too small to surface and the framing risk isn't worth it). Score-breakdown tooltip line: 'Liquidity Pressure: +22' (never 'Bond' / 'Jail' / 'Arrest'). Lead detail drawer category label: 'Cash Motivation Signals' — same drawer section as Tax Delinquency and Lien/Judgment. The underlying data row in the drawer reads 'Distress event detected · 7 days ago' with NO charges, NO bond dollar amount, NO booking number, NO mugshot, NO court date, NO arresting agency. Admin/operator-only role (Clerk role:'admin' or 'ops') gets a SECOND drawer section labeled 'Source Detail (Internal)' that shows: county source slug (jso/hcso/etc.), booking date, bond amount range (bucketed: <$5k / $5–25k / $25k+, not exact), match confidence %, and a 'View source' link to the sheriff's public record URL — but still NEVER charges or mugshot in our UI. Charges and mugshots are intentionally NOT mirrored to our DB beyond the scrape-cache layer (see privacyFilters)."
privacyFilters: §119.071(2)(j) and (4)(d) exempt-class filter: hard-block any record whose name matches our FL exempt-occupation dictionary (LEO, judge, prosecutor, victim/witness flags) — even if the sheriff site leaked it. Maintain `flipops.ExemptOccupationDictionary` table with weekly refresh from FDLE published categories.

Marsy's Law (FL Const. Art. I §16(b)) victim suppression: any row where charge code starts with victim-of-violence statutes (chapters 741, 784 partial, 794, 800, 827) is flagged for human review before contributing to score. Default = do-not-score until reviewed.

Juvenile exclusion: hard-drop any row where computed age at booking < 18 (DOB-derived from MDCR/HCSO where DOB present; for JSO/PBSO where DOB is suppressed, name-collision-with-known-minor check via voter-file age).

Mugshot suppression: even if scraped (MDCR base64, OCFL base64, JSO CDN), mugshots are NEVER persisted past the scrape worker. Worker extracts only the bytes-exist boolean for QA; image bytes are deleted after parse. Investor UI has no mugshot field, no admin role has access, no API exposes the field.

Charges suppression in investor UI: charge codes/descriptions are stored in `flipops.JailBookingChargeRaw` for legal audit (proving we did NOT scrape sealed/expunged data) but are NEVER returned from any investor-facing API endpoint. Only `count_of_charges` and `bond_amount_bucket` may surface in admin views.

Right-to-be-forgotten endpoint: POST /api/admin/jail-booking/suppress with bookingId or inmateNumber sets `suppressed=true` and removes that row's contribution from cached scores within 5 minutes. Audit logged.

90-day decay floor: any jail signal older than 730 days (2 years) contributes 0 — the row stays in DB for analytics but does not score. Prevents perpetual stigma from a 5-year-old single misdemeanor booking.

Sealed/expunged re-check: weekly cron polls FDLE Seal & Expunge bulk feed; any matched bookingId is marked sealed=true and its score contribution drops to 0 immediately (not waiting for normal decay).

Public-record-attribution: investor UI never shows 'arrest', 'booking', 'jail', 'inmate', or 'bond' as a label. Score breakdown reads 'Liquidity pressure event' only. This protects both the homeowner from premature stigma and us from a defamation/false-light-tort vector if our match confidence was wrong.
aggregationDesign.rescoringPolicy: "Hybrid: immediate for ACTIVE_BOND_IN_CUSTODY (the in-custody window is the highest-leverage moment — a delayed score is a missed lead), batch for all other jail signals. Specifically: when a new InmateBooking row is inserted with `releaseDate IS NULL` AND matchConfidence >= 0.78 AND a Parcel match exists, fire a synchronous re-score on that Parcel within the same DB transaction (debounced 30s per parcel to prevent thrash on multi-charge bookings that insert 3-5 charge rows back-to-back). For all other inserts (released bookings, recidivism updates), enqueue to the existing nightly distress-rescore cron job that already runs daily at 8 AM ET (`cron:data-refresh`). Re-score on release-event too: when a previously in-custody row gets a releaseDate set (release-log scraper), trigger immediate downgrade from ACTIVE_BOND_IN_CUSTODY (22) → POSTED_CASH_BOND_RECENT (15) within the 30s debounce window. Score deltas of >=5 points trigger a notification row in `flipops.Notification` so the investor sees 'Lead score changed: +22' in their dashboard widget."
aggregationDesign.ttlDecayFunction: "Piecewise linear with three regimes, keyed on days since booking event (for ACTIVE_BOND_IN_CUSTODY) or days since release (for POSTED_CASH_BOND_RECENT and RELEASED_ROR): REGIME A (days 0–7): full weight × 1.0 — acute window, no decay. REGIME B (days 8–60): linear decay from 1.0 → 0.5 (i.e., contribution = weight × (1.0 − (day−7) × 0.5/53)). REGIME C (days 61–365): linear decay from 0.5 → 0.1. REGIME D (days 366–730): linear decay from 0.1 → 0.0. REGIME E (day 730+): 0 contribution (hard floor — see privacyFilters). ACTIVE_BOND_IN_CUSTODY uses days-since-booking (not release) because the in-custody clock IS the urgency; if still in custody at day 60 the bond is likely NO BOND / felony and the cash-motivation signal is weaker (they're not getting out via money), so decay is appropriate. RECIDIVISM uses a different rule: count of bookings in trailing 365 days, no per-event decay — the count itself IS the signal. Decay formula in code: `contribution = baseWeight * Math.max(0, Math.min(1, regimeMultiplier(daysSince)))`."

aggregationDesign.rationale: "The user's instinct is correct: an unpaid bond is among the highest cash-motivation signals available in public-record data — arguably higher than a tax-lien (20pts) on pure liquidity-urgency, because the cash-need clock is hours/days not 90+ days. But the data-quality penalty (name-only matching, no address from JSO/HCSO/BSO/PBSO) and the legal/UX framing risk (defamation, false-light, premature stigma, §119.071 exempt-class leakage) force us to rank ACTIVE_BOND_IN_CUSTODY at 22 — just below Pre-Foreclosure/Auction (25) and slightly above Lien (20). The decomposition into ACTIVE/POSTED/ROR mirrors the actual cash-flow event: ACTIVE = liquidity gap NOW, POSTED = liquidity gap CLOSED LAST WEEK, ROR = no cash event. Mutual-exclusivity within the jail channel + a 30-pt category cap prevents one charge-heavy multi-warrant booking (like the Miami-Dade SMITH example with 7 warrants) from running away with the score. Time decay is non-linear-piecewise because cash-motivation signals are SHARPLY peaked (0–7 days the seller is most desperate) and then half-life around 60 days. The 730-day floor + sealed-records sync is a compliance must-have, not optional. UI copy MUST be neutral ('Liquidity Pressure', 'Cash Motivation') because (a) defamation risk if our 0.78-confidence match is wrong, (b) FL Marsy's Law & §119.071 expectation that we won't aggregate exempt records, (c) cleaner mental model for investors who don't need to know the source to act on the score. Admin-only source-detail drawer keeps ops auditability without leaking arrest data into customer UI. Match-confidence floor of 0.78 is calibrated to NAME_FUZZY+OWNER_OCCUPIED being the weakest scoring tier — anything lower is just noise and false positives at scale (top-1000 surnames in Miami-Dade will hit thousands of FL homeowners named SMITH). Re-score-immediate-on-in-custody is the load-bearing operational choice: the in-custody window is when the lead is hottest, and a 12-hour batch delay = a wholesaler in the same county got there first."
openQuestions: Should we expose the jail channel AT ALL to free-tier users, or gate it behind Scale/Accelerator/Partner like platform vendors? Argument for gating: this signal is high-leverage AND has the highest ethical/legal sensitivity — premium tiers carry more contractual liability protection. Argument against: distress signals are core product value, gating fragments the experience.

What's our policy when an investor sends outreach (SMS/letter) to a lead whose top signal is jail-channel and the owner is actually in custody (no one home to receive mail)? Should the outreach module suppress send for ACTIVE_BOND_IN_CUSTODY leads or instead recommend skip-trace to a relative? This is a UX decision the campaigns module owners need to weigh in on.

Do we need a §119.071 / Marsy's Law legal review BEFORE shipping this even with neutral copy? FL Statute is permissive for ingestion of public arrest records, but our score-aggregation + commercial use case may trigger a different analysis than typical journalism / records-request scenarios. Recommend running this design past outside FL counsel before turning on the JSO/MDCR scrapers in prod.

Match confidence floor of 0.78 is a calibration guess — we should backtest against a labeled set (manually verified 200 jail-booking-to-parcel matches across top-5 metros) and tune to hit precision >= 0.92 / recall >= 0.70. Owe this to F2 phase as a deliverable.

Should ROR (4pts) even be in the model? If we hide it from the investor UI anyway, the only value is admin-side context. Worth dropping to simplify the algorithm unless backtesting shows ROR-only correlates with future bookings (recidivism predictor).

Cross-county recidivism: an inmateNumber from JSO is NOT the same as an IDS from MDCR. Do we build a cross-county person-resolution layer (name + DOB + race + gender + height fingerprint) or accept per-county recidivism only? Per-county is simpler; cross-county catches snowbirds and serial-county-hoppers but adds entity-resolution complexity.

Mugshot retention: probes show OCFL and MDCR embed mugshots as base64 in JSON responses. Even if we never persist them, our scrape worker has them in memory for ~milliseconds. Is that a CCPA/privacy attack-surface concern? Recommend the scraper explicitly strips IMAGE / mugshot fields BEFORE the parse phase, never even deserializing them.

HCSO captcha cost: at 1 search per 30 min × 26 surname-letter sweeps = 1,248 captcha solves per day for Hillsborough alone. At 2captcha $2.99/1k that's $3.73/day = $1,360/year just for HCSO. Is that worth it relative to the ~120 bookings/day signal volume? Maybe drop HCSO from the v1 launch and just enable JSO + OCFL + PBSO (the three easiest sources).
